_comment: A fictional profile, deliberately nothing like the author's: a longer career starting in the nineties, a folded gap, no volunteering lane, three projects, one role spanning two cities by sub-range, one role with no place at all, and one hidden entry.

identity.name: Marisol Okonkwo-Reyes
identity.headline: Coastal Hydrologist · Flood Risk Modelling
identity.summary: Hydrologist with twenty-four years turning tide gauges, rainfall radar and bathymetry into flood risk somebody can plan around. I build the whole chain: the hydraulic model, the calibration against real gauge records, and the maps a city council will actually act on.
identity.about: I work on the unglamorous half of climate adaptation — the part where a model has to survive contact with a drainage network nobody has surveyed since 1970. Every number I publish carries its uncertainty band, because a flood map without one gets read as a promise.

contact.h2: it is not supposed to go?
contact.p: I'd like to hear about it. I'm based in Porto and work across the Atlantic coast.

entries.title: Research Hydrologist
entries.note: Calibrated estuary models against forty years of gauge records for the Dutch coastal defence programme.

entries.title: Senior Flood Risk Modeller
entries.note: Two postings in one role: the Lisbon estuary programme, then the Recife drainage retrofit.

entries.title: Independent Consultant
entries.note: Fully remote across eleven countries; no office worth putting on a map.

entries.title: Principal Hydrologist
entries.note: Leads the open flood-atlas programme for the Iberian Atlantic coast.

entries.title: Weekend Bar Work
entries.note: Paid for the PhD. Not part of the story I want to tell.

work.title: An open flood atlas for the Iberian Atlantic coast
work.blurb: Every stretch of coast from Bayonne to Cádiz, modelled at 5m and published with its uncertainty band rather than as a single line on a map.
bullets: Calibrated against 38 tide gauges; median error 6cm at the annual maximum.
Published the uncertainty raster alongside every depth raster, because a bare depth map gets read as a promise.
Adopted by four municipal planning departments in the first year.

work.title: Rescuing sixty years of paper tide records
work.blurb: Handwritten gauge sheets from 1961 onwards, scanned, read and reconciled against the modern digital record.
bullets: Recovered 2.1 million readings that existed only on paper.
Hand-checked a stratified 2% sample rather than trusting the model's own confidence.

work.title: A drainage twin for a city with no drainage survey
work.blurb: Inferring a storm network's topology from where the water actually goes, when nobody has the plans any more.
bullets: Treats the network as the unknown and the flooding as the observation.

beyond: Field seasons with the people who use the maps
